## Conjugate Priors and Choosing Your Prior {#sec-conjugate-priors}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Sources for this section"}

|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Gregory Gundersen, "Conjugacy in Bayesian Inference" (2019)](https://gregorygundersen.com/blog/2019/03/16/conjugacy/) | Benefits of conjugacy, sequential learning |
| 2 | [Wikipedia: Conjugate Prior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_prior) | Complete table of conjugate families |

In the previous sections, you saw how Bayes' theorem turns a prior and a likelihood into a posterior. The Beta-Binomial example (return rate) and the Dirichlet-Categorical example (star ratings) both had a convenient property: the posterior came out in a recognizable closed form. That convenience was not an accident. We chose priors from special families that pair naturally with their corresponding likelihoods. These special families are called *conjugate priors*, and understanding them gives you both a computational shortcut and a conceptual framework for how data updates beliefs.

But the headphones problem has five quantities, not two. We have already derived posteriors for the return rate and the star ratings. What about the other three: return reasons (also categorical), customer questions per day (count data), and battery life (continuous)? This section tackles all five conjugate families in parallel, applies each one to its corresponding headphones quantity, and develops a framework for choosing priors.

### What Conjugacy Means

Think back to the headphones example. You started with a Beta(2, 12) prior for the return rate, observed Binomial data, and got a Beta posterior. You plugged in numbers and read off the answer directly. No integrals, no numerical approximation. Why did that work so cleanly? Because the Beta distribution is *conjugate* to the Binomial likelihood. The same happened with the Dirichlet-Categorical pair for star ratings. The precise definition is straightforward:

A prior distribution $p(\theta)$ is *conjugate* to a likelihood $p(x \mid \theta)$ if the resulting posterior $p(\theta \mid x)$ belongs to the same distributional family as the prior. The posterior has the same functional form; only its parameters change. As [MIT 18.05 Lec 15](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/) puts it: "A prior is conjugate to a likelihood if the posterior is the same type of distribution as the prior. Updating becomes algebra instead of calculus."

Why does conjugacy matter? Three practical benefits stand out.

Three practical benefits stand out. First, you never need to evaluate the normalizing integral in Bayes' theorem. Second, you can read off the posterior parameters directly from the prior parameters and the data summary. Third, as [Gundersen (2019)](https://gregorygundersen.com/blog/2019/03/16/conjugacy/) explains, conjugacy enables *sequential updating*: after observing one batch of data and computing a posterior, that posterior becomes the prior for the next batch. Because the posterior stays in the same family, you can keep feeding in data indefinitely without changing your computational machinery.

The cost of conjugacy is a constraint on flexibility. Conjugate priors express a specific shape of belief, and real prior knowledge may not fit neatly into that shape. We return to this limitation at the end of the section.

### The Major Conjugate Families

The table below lists the four conjugate families that cover our five headphones quantities (the Dirichlet-Categorical serves double duty for star ratings and return reasons). Each row shows the prior family, the likelihood it pairs with, the resulting posterior family, the update rule, and which headphones quantity it handles. Refer to [Wikipedia: Conjugate Prior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_prior) and [Cook's Compendium of Conjugate Priors (2009)](https://www.johndcook.com/CompendiumOfConjugatePriors.pdf) for the complete catalog.

| Prior | Likelihood | Posterior | Update Rule | Headphones Quantity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$ | $\text{Binomial}(n, \theta)$ | $\text{Beta}(\alpha + k,\; \beta + n - k)$ | Add returns to $\alpha$, non-returns to $\beta$ | **Return rate** |
| $\text{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ | $\text{Categorical}(\mathbf{p})$ | $\text{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol{\alpha} + \mathbf{n})$ | Add category counts to concentration parameters | **Star ratings, Return reasons** |
| $\text{Gamma}(s, r)$ | $\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ | $\text{Gamma}(s + \sum y_i,\; r + n)$ | Add total count to $s$, number of observations to $r$ | **Questions/day** |
| $\text{Normal}(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)$ | $\text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ (known $\sigma^2$) | $\text{Normal}(\mu_{\text{post}}, \sigma_{\text{post}}^2)$ | Precision-weighted average of prior and data means | **Battery life** |

The pattern across all four rows is the same: the data summary (counts, sums, sample means) gets absorbed into the prior's parameters. The posterior is just the prior "plus evidence." In each case, the exponents or sufficient statistics from the likelihood combine additively with the prior's hyperparameters.

::: {.exercise-mcq correct="B"}

You observe 7 days of customer-question counts for the headphones and want to update your Gamma(4, 2) prior to a posterior. Which of the following correctly describes the Gamma-Poisson conjugate update?

- Add the sample mean to the shape parameter and divide the rate parameter by n
- Add the total count across all days to the shape parameter and add the number of days to the rate parameter
- Replace the shape parameter with the sample mean and replace the rate parameter with the sample variance
- Multiply the shape parameter by the number of days and leave the rate parameter unchanged

::: {.feedback-correct}
Correct. The Gamma-Poisson update adds the total observed count to the prior shape parameter s and adds the number of observation periods to the prior rate parameter r. If you observe 7 days with a total of 14 questions, the posterior is Gamma(4 + 14, 2 + 7) = Gamma(18, 9). The sufficient statistics for the Poisson likelihood are the total count and the number of observations, which map directly onto the Gamma's two parameters.
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
The Gamma-Poisson update has a specific structure: the total count (not the mean) adds to the shape parameter, and the number of observations (not the variance or a divisor) adds to the rate parameter. Option A incorrectly uses the sample mean and divides. Option C replaces rather than adds, destroying the prior information. Option D only modifies one parameter and uses multiplication instead of addition. The conjugate update always combines prior parameters and data summaries additively.
:::

:::

### Worked Example: Normal-Normal (Battery Life)

The manufacturer claims these headphones have a 30-hour battery life. Five reviewers reported battery lives of 28, 31, 29, 32, and 30 hours. The parameter $\mu$ is the true mean battery life. We model each measurement as $Y_i \mid \mu \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with known measurement variance $\sigma^2 = 4$ (corresponding to $\sigma = 2$ hours). Your prior belief, based on experience with similar electronics, is that battery life claims are usually close to reality: $\mu \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_0 = 30,\; \sigma_0^2 = 4)$.

The conjugate update for the Normal-Normal model proceeds in two steps. First, compute the posterior variance using the *precision-addition* rule. Precision is the reciprocal of variance, so the prior precision is $1/\sigma_0^2$ and the data precision is $n/\sigma^2$:

$$
\sigma_{\text{post}}^2 = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{5}{4}} = \frac{1}{0.25 + 1.25} = \frac{1}{1.5} \approx 0.667.
$$ {#eq-normal-posterior-variance}

The posterior precision is the sum of the prior precision and the data precision. This precision-addition rule is the core insight: *more information (from either source) always increases precision*.

Second, compute the posterior mean as a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean. The sample mean is $\bar{y} = (28 + 31 + 29 + 32 + 30)/5 = 30.0$.

$$
\mu_{\text{post}} = \sigma_{\text{post}}^2 \left( \frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n\bar{y}}{\sigma^2} \right) = 0.667 \times \left( \frac{30}{4} + \frac{5 \times 30}{4} \right) = 0.667 \times (7.5 + 37.5) = 0.667 \times 45 = 30.0.
$$ {#eq-normal-posterior-mean}

The posterior is $\text{Normal}(30.0,\; 0.667)$, with a standard deviation of about $0.82$ hours. In this case, the prior mean and the sample mean agree (both are 30.0), so the posterior mean is also 30.0. The posterior variance is much smaller than either the prior variance (4.0) or the data variance (4.0/5 = 0.8), because the posterior precision is the *sum* of the prior and data precisions. The prior carried precision 0.25; the data carried precision 1.25; the posterior carries precision 1.5. Five measurements plus the prior produced a posterior standard deviation under 1 hour, tight enough to be confident the true mean is close to 30 hours.

The following plot visualizes the three distributions. Because the prior mean and sample mean happen to agree, the three curves are centered at the same point; the visual payoff is seeing the *precision addition* in action.

```{python}
#| output: false
#| error: true
#| warning: false
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import hvplot.pandas
import holoviews as hv
from scipy import stats
hv.extension('bokeh')

hvplot_opts = dict(width=750, height=450, grid=True)
hv_opts = dict(
    show_grid=True,
    default_tools=['hover', 'save', 'pan', 'box_zoom', 'reset', 'wheel_zoom'],
    active_tools=['pan'],
)

x = np.linspace(24, 36, 500)

prior_pdf = stats.norm.pdf(x, 30, np.sqrt(4))
data_pdf = stats.norm.pdf(x, 30, np.sqrt(4/5))
posterior_pdf = stats.norm.pdf(x, 30, np.sqrt(0.667))

df_nn = pd.DataFrame({
    'Battery life (hours)': np.tile(x, 3),
    'Density': np.concatenate([prior_pdf, data_pdf, posterior_pdf]),
    'Distribution': (
        ['Prior: N(30, 4)'] * len(x)
        + ['Data: N(30, 0.8)'] * len(x)
        + ['Posterior: N(30, 0.667)'] * len(x)
    ),
})

nn_plot = df_nn.hvplot.line(
    x='Battery life (hours)', y='Density', by='Distribution',
    **hvplot_opts,
    xlabel='μ (mean battery life, hours)',
    ylabel='Density',
    title='Normal-Normal Update: Precision Addition',
    line_width=2.5,
    color=['#6366F1', '#F59E0B', '#10B981'],
).opts(**hv_opts)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-normal-normal-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Normal-Normal Bayesian update for battery life. The prior N(30, 4) is broad (σ = 2 hours). The sampling distribution of the mean N(30, 0.8) is narrower. The posterior N(30, 0.667) is narrower still, because posterior precision equals prior precision plus data precision: 0.25 + 1.25 = 1.5."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from bokeh.io import output_notebook, show
import holoviews as hv
output_notebook(hide_banner=True)
show(hv.render(nn_plot, backend='bokeh'))
```

This precision-weighted averaging is what makes the Normal-Normal pair so intuitive. The posterior always lies between the prior mean and the sample mean, pulled toward whichever source carries more precision. Following [Bayes Rules Ch5 (2022)](https://www.bayesrulesbook.com/chapter-5), the posterior mean weight on the data is $n\tau^2 / (n\tau^2 + \sigma^2)$, which equals $5 \times 4 / (5 \times 4 + 4) = 20/24 \approx 0.83$. With five observations, the data contributes 83% of the total evidence.

::: {.exercise-fillin}

Suppose a rival headphones product has battery life measurements from 8 reviewers with a sample mean of 27.5 hours. You use the same Normal-Normal setup: known variance of 4 and a Normal(30, 4) prior. Work through the posterior:

1. The prior precision is 1 divided by 4, which equals 0.25.
2. The data precision is 8 divided by 4, which equals 2.0.
3. The posterior precision is 0.25 plus 2.0, giving 2.25. The posterior variance is 1 divided by 2.25, approximately 0.444.
4. The posterior mean weights the prior mean by prior precision and the sample mean by data precision. The prior term is 30 times 0.25 = 7.5 and the data term is 27.5 times 2.0 = 55.
5. Adding: 7.5 plus 55 equals 62.5. Multiplying by the posterior variance: the posterior mean is approximately {B|A: 30.0|B: 27.8|C: 28.75}.

::: {.fillin-feedback}
**Correct: B (27.8).** The posterior mean is 0.444 times 62.5 = 27.78, approximately 27.8 hours. Because the data precision (2.0) is eight times larger than the prior precision (0.25), the posterior mean is pulled strongly toward the sample mean of 27.5 rather than the prior mean of 30. The data contributes 2.0/2.25 = 89% of the weight. This is a case where the data contradicts the manufacturer's claim, and the posterior reflects that disagreement.
:::

:::

### Gamma-Poisson: Customer Questions Per Day

The headphones listing shows customer questions arriving at about 2 per day. You observe the daily counts over 7 days: $y_1, \ldots, y_7$, giving a total of $\sum y_i = 14$ questions and a sample mean of $\bar{y} = 2.0$. The parameter $\lambda > 0$ is the true question rate (expected questions per day). Following the derivation in [Bayes Rules Ch5 (2022)](https://www.bayesrulesbook.com/chapter-5), assign a Gamma prior $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(s = 4, r = 2)$ with mean $s/r = 2$ questions per day. This prior reflects your belief that 1-3 questions per day is typical for products in this category. Each daily count follows $Y_i \mid \lambda \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, so the likelihood is proportional to $\lambda^{\sum y_i} e^{-n\lambda}$. Multiplying by the Gamma prior gives

$$
p(\lambda \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \propto \lambda^{s + \sum y_i - 1} \, e^{-(r+n)\lambda},
$$

which is the *kernel* of a $\text{Gamma}(s + \sum y_i, \; r + n)$ distribution. (The kernel is the part of the density that identifies the distributional family, ignoring normalizing constants.) For our headphones data: $\text{Gamma}(4, 2)$ prior + Poisson observations ($\sum y_i = 14$, $n = 7$) yields $\text{Gamma}(4 + 14, 2 + 7) = \text{Gamma}(18, 9)$. The update rule adds the total count to $s$ and the number of observations to $r$. The posterior mean is

$$
E[\lambda \mid \boldsymbol{y}] = \frac{s + \sum y_i}{r + n} = \frac{18}{9} = 2.0 = \frac{r}{r+n} \cdot \frac{s}{r} + \frac{n}{r+n} \cdot \bar{y},
$$

where $s/r = 2$ is the prior mean and $\bar{y} = 14/7 = 2.0$ is the sample mean (the MLE). The posterior mean equals both the prior mean and the MLE in this case, because they happen to agree. Once again, the posterior mean is a convex combination of the prior mean and the MLE, with weights governed by the ratio of prior pseudo-observations $r$ to actual observations $n$. This convex-combination structure is the same *linear Bayes* property we saw in the Beta-Binomial case.

The following plot shows the Gamma-Poisson update visually. Unlike the symmetric Normal-Normal, the Gamma distribution is right-skewed, so the curves have a distinctive asymmetric shape.

```{python}
#| output: false
#| error: true
#| warning: false
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import hvplot.pandas
import holoviews as hv
from scipy import stats
hv.extension('bokeh')

hvplot_opts = dict(width=750, height=450, grid=True)
hv_opts = dict(
    show_grid=True,
    default_tools=['hover', 'save', 'pan', 'box_zoom', 'reset', 'wheel_zoom'],
    active_tools=['pan'],
)

lam = np.linspace(0.01, 6.0, 500)

prior_pdf = stats.gamma.pdf(lam, a=4, scale=1/2)

raw_likelihood = np.exp(14 * np.log(lam) - 7 * lam)
likelihood_normalized = raw_likelihood / np.trapz(raw_likelihood, lam)

posterior_pdf = stats.gamma.pdf(lam, a=18, scale=1/9)

df_gp = pd.DataFrame({
    'λ': np.tile(lam, 3),
    'Density': np.concatenate([prior_pdf, likelihood_normalized, posterior_pdf]),
    'Distribution': (
        ['Prior: Gamma(4, 2)'] * len(lam)
        + ['Likelihood (normalized)'] * len(lam)
        + ['Posterior: Gamma(18, 9)'] * len(lam)
    ),
})

gp_plot = df_gp.hvplot.line(
    x='λ', y='Density', by='Distribution',
    **hvplot_opts,
    xlabel='λ (questions per day)',
    ylabel='Density',
    title='Gamma-Poisson Update: Customer Questions Per Day',
    line_width=2.5,
    color=['#6366F1', '#F59E0B', '#10B981'],
).opts(**hv_opts)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-gamma-poisson-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Gamma-Poisson Bayesian update for customer questions per day. The Gamma(4, 2) prior (mean = 2) is broad and right-skewed. The normalized Poisson likelihood concentrates near the sample mean of 2.0. The posterior Gamma(18, 9) is narrower and symmetric-looking because the large shape parameter makes the Gamma approximately Normal."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from bokeh.io import output_notebook, show
import holoviews as hv
output_notebook(hide_banner=True)
```

### All Five Quantities: The Completed Posterior Table

We now have conjugate posteriors for all five headphones quantities. The table below summarizes the prior, data, and posterior for each:

| Quantity | Prior | Data | Posterior | Posterior Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Return rate** | Beta(2, 12) | 3 returns / 20 buyers | Beta(5, 29) | 0.147 |
| **Star ratings** | Dir(1,1,1,1,1) | counts (2,1,2,5,10) | Dir(3,2,3,6,11) | (0.12, 0.08, 0.12, 0.24, 0.44) |
| **Return reasons** | Dir(1,1,1,1,1) | counts (1,1,1,0,0) | Dir(2,2,2,1,1) | (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125) |
| **Questions/day** | Gamma(4, 2) | $\sum y_i = 14$, $n = 7$ | Gamma(18, 9) | 2.0 |
| **Battery life** | Normal(30, 4) | $\bar{y} = 30$, $n = 5$ | Normal(30.0, 0.667) | 30.0 |

Every row was computed using the same recipe: multiply prior by likelihood, collect sufficient statistics into the prior's parameters, and read off the result. The observation spaces are different (binary, categorical, counts, continuous), the parameter spaces are different ($[0,1]$, simplex, positive reals, all reals), and the specific distributions are different. But the Bayesian updating machinery is identical in structure. This structural uniformity is the payoff of the conjugate prior framework.

### Prior Sensitivity: Same Data, Different Beliefs

The Normal-Normal example had a single prior. But what happens when you are less sure about the prior? To see how the choice of prior affects the posterior, consider the return rate Beta-Binomial problem from @sec-bayesian-updating: 3 returns out of 20 buyers. The following plot shows four different priors and their resulting posteriors, all conditioned on the same data.

::: {.exercise-predict correct="C"}

Before seeing the sensitivity plot, make a prediction. Suppose you use four different priors for the headphones return rate, all with the same 3/20 observed data. The four priors are: Beta(1,1) uniform, Beta(0.5, 0.5) Jeffreys, Beta(2, 12) mild prior experience, and Beta(4, 20) strong belief. How will the four posteriors compare?

- All four posteriors will be nearly identical, because 20 observations are enough to overwhelm any prior
- The four posteriors will have completely different peaks and spread, with no convergence
- The weaker priors (uniform and Jeffreys) will produce nearly identical posteriors, while the strong prior Beta(4, 20) will noticeably shift the posterior peak away from the MLE

::: {.predict-reveal}
**The answer is C.** The uniform Beta(1,1) and Jeffreys Beta(0.5, 0.5) priors are so weak that 20 observations dominate them, producing posteriors that are nearly identical and centered near the MLE of 0.15. But the strong Beta(4, 20) prior contributes the equivalent of 24 pseudo-observations, which is comparable to the 20 real data points. With nearly equal "weight," the strong prior noticeably pulls the posterior peak toward its own mean of 0.167. Twenty observations is enough to wash out weak priors but not strong ones. Scroll down to @fig-prior-sensitivity to see the exact curves.
:::

:::

```{python}
#| output: false
#| error: true
#| warning: false
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import hvplot.pandas
import holoviews as hv
hv.extension('bokeh')

theta = np.linspace(0, 1, 500)
k, n = 3, 20

priors = {
    "Beta(1,1) Uniform": (1, 1),
    "Beta(2,12) Prior experience": (2, 12),
    "Beta(4,20) Strong belief": (4, 20),
    "Beta(0.5,0.5) Jeffreys": (0.5, 0.5),
}

rows = []
for label, (a, b) in priors.items():
    prior_pdf = stats.beta.pdf(theta, a, b)
    post_a, post_b = a + k, b + n - k
    post_pdf = stats.beta.pdf(theta, post_a, post_b)
    for t, pr, po in zip(theta, prior_pdf, post_pdf):
        rows.append({"θ": t, "Density": pr, "Type": "Prior", "Prior choice": label})
        rows.append({"θ": t, "Density": po, "Type": "Posterior", "Prior choice": label})

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

hvplot_opts = dict(width=750, height=420, grid=True)
hv_opts = dict(
    show_grid=True,
    default_tools=['hover', 'save', 'pan', 'box_zoom', 'reset', 'wheel_zoom'],
    active_tools=['pan'],
)

prior_plot = (
    df[df["Type"] == "Prior"]
    .hvplot.line(x="θ", y="Density", by="Prior choice", **hvplot_opts, line_width=2, line_dash="dashed", title="Prior distributions", ylabel="Density")
    .opts(**hv_opts)
)

posterior_plot = (
    df[df["Type"] == "Posterior"]
    .hvplot.line(x="θ", y="Density", by="Prior choice", **hvplot_opts, line_width=2.5, title="Posterior distributions (15/20 observed)", ylabel="Density")
    .opts(**hv_opts)
)

final_plot = (prior_plot + posterior_plot).cols(1)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-prior-sensitivity
#| fig-cap: "Prior sensitivity analysis. Top: four different prior distributions for the return rate θ. Bottom: the corresponding posteriors after observing 3 returns in 20 buyers. The posteriors converge toward each other, but the strong Beta(4,20) prior still shifts the peak."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from bokeh.io import output_notebook, show
import holoviews as hv
output_notebook(hide_banner=True)
show(hv.render(final_plot, backend='bokeh'))
```

Four lessons emerge from @fig-prior-sensitivity. First, the uniform prior $\text{Beta}(1,1)$ and the Jeffreys prior $\text{Beta}(0.5, 0.5)$ produce nearly identical posteriors, both centered near $\theta = 0.15$. Second, the prior-experience prior $\text{Beta}(2,12)$ nudges the posterior only slightly, since its mean of 0.143 is close to the MLE of 0.15. Third, the strong prior $\text{Beta}(4,20)$ pulls the posterior peak noticeably toward $\theta = 0.167$. Fourth, with only 20 observations, the strong prior still exerts meaningful influence. With 200 observations, even that strong prior would be overwhelmed.

**The key takeaway:** with enough data, the posterior becomes insensitive to the prior. With limited data, the prior matters. You should examine how sensitive your conclusions are to the prior choice.

### A Practical Framework for Choosing Priors

If conjugacy tells you the *form* of the prior, prior selection tells you *which parameters to set*. Three broad strategies exist, ordered from most to least informative.

**Informative priors** encode genuine domain knowledge. Suppose you have browsed similar products in this category across 50 listings on Amazon and seen return rates around 0.10 with a standard deviation of 0.05. You can encode this belief directly as a Beta prior whose mean and variance match those values. Informative priors are the most powerful tool in the Bayesian toolkit when the knowledge is real, but they require honest calibration. Overstating your certainty biases the posterior. Understating it wastes information.

**Weakly informative priors** constrain the parameter to a reasonable range without committing to a precise value. [Gelman (2009)](https://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/jeffreys.pdf) advocates this approach as the practical default: "seemingly noninformative distributions can sometimes have strong and undesirable implications." He argues for priors that "attempt to let the data speak while being strong enough to exclude various 'unphysical' possibilities which, if not blocked, can take over a posterior distribution in settings with sparse data."

For a return rate, $\text{Beta}(2, 8)$ says "probably somewhere between 5% and 30%, but I'm not sure where." For a regression coefficient, $\text{Normal}(0, 10)$ says "probably not enormous, but could be positive or negative." The prior rules out absurd values (like a return rate of 99%) without pretending to know the truth. This strategy works well because it regularizes estimation without dominating the data.

**"Uninformative" priors** aim to let the data speak entirely for themselves. The most common attempt is the flat (uniform) prior. But here is the problem:

::: {.callout-warning}
**Common Misconception: Flat priors are non-informative.**

A uniform prior on $\theta$ is *not* uniform on $\log(\theta)$ or $\theta^2$. If you reparametrize the problem, the "flat" prior becomes informative in the new parametrization. As [Gelman (2009)](https://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/jeffreys.pdf) argues, "it can be notoriously difficult to choose among noninformative priors; and, even more importantly, seemingly noninformative distributions can sometimes have strong and undesirable implications." He recommends *weakly informative* priors that are "strong enough to exclude various 'unphysical' possibilities" rather than flat priors that create an illusion of objectivity.
:::

The *Jeffreys prior* offers a principled alternative to flat priors. The core problem is that a flat prior on $\theta$ is not flat on $\log(\theta)$ or $\theta^2$, so you need a prior whose shape adjusts automatically under reparametrization. The Jeffreys prior does exactly that: it is defined as $p(\theta) \propto \sqrt{I(\theta)}$ and is *invariant under reparametrization*. If you transform $\theta \to \phi(\theta)$, the Jeffreys prior in $\phi$-space is exactly what you get by transforming the Jeffreys prior in $\theta$-space.

The quantity $I(\theta)$ is the *Fisher information*, a measure of how sharply the log-likelihood $p(x \mid \theta)$ curves around $\theta$. When the likelihood is sharply peaked, $I(\theta)$ is large and the data are highly informative about $\theta$. For the Bernoulli model, the Jeffreys prior works out to $\text{Beta}(0.5, 0.5)$. For the Normal mean with known variance, the Jeffreys prior is a uniform (improper) prior on $\mu$. The Jeffreys prior is mathematically elegant, but it has two drawbacks: (a) it can produce improper posteriors in some models, and (b) it does not incorporate domain knowledge. For these reasons, weakly informative priors are preferred in practice.

The following decision framework, based on the recommendations in [Gelman et al.](https://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/jeffreys.pdf), summarizes these strategies:

1. **Do you have genuine domain expertise?** Use an *informative* prior. Encode what you know, and run a sensitivity analysis to check that your conclusions are robust.
2. **Are you uncertain but want regularization?** Use a *weakly informative* prior. Set broad but bounded parameters that rule out implausible values.
3. **Do you want a "default" prior for comparison?** Use the *Jeffreys* prior for that model, but check that the posterior is proper.
4. **Always run a prior sensitivity analysis.** Plot the posterior under 2-3 different priors (as in @fig-prior-sensitivity) and verify that your substantive conclusions do not hinge on the prior choice.

::: {.exercise-mcq correct="C"}

You are modeling a new product's return rate and have no domain expertise. A colleague suggests using a Beta(1, 1) flat prior "to be objective." Based on the framework for choosing priors, what is the best response?

- Use Beta(1, 1) because it encodes no assumptions and lets the data speak
- Use the Jeffreys prior Beta(0.5, 0.5) because it is provably non-informative in all parametrizations
- Use a weakly informative prior like Beta(2, 8) because it rules out implausible extremes (like 99% return rates) while still letting the data dominate, and then run a sensitivity analysis
- Use an informative prior based on your gut feeling about the product

::: {.feedback-correct}
Correct. Weakly informative priors are the recommended default when you lack strong domain expertise. A flat prior like Beta(1,1) is not truly "objective" because it becomes informative under reparametrization (e.g., it is not flat on the log-odds scale). The Jeffreys prior Beta(0.5, 0.5) solves the reparametrization problem but can produce improper posteriors in some models and does not prevent implausible values from dominating in sparse-data settings. A weakly informative prior like Beta(2, 8) constrains the return rate to a plausible range without pretending to know the exact value. Running a sensitivity analysis (comparing posteriors under 2-3 priors) confirms that your conclusions are robust.
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
Option A ignores the reparametrization problem: a flat prior on the return rate is not flat on the log-odds, so "objectivity" is illusory. Option B is closer but overstates the Jeffreys prior's universality; it can produce improper posteriors and does not incorporate even soft constraints. Option D conflates gut feeling with calibrated domain knowledge; informative priors require genuine expertise, not guesses. The practical recommendation is a weakly informative prior plus sensitivity analysis.
:::

:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Think Hard:** In what sense is ridge regression "secretly Bayesian"? What prior does it correspond to?

Ridge regression minimizes $\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta})^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2$. The penalty term $\lambda \|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2$ is equivalent to placing a $\text{Normal}(0, 1/\lambda)$ prior on each coefficient $\beta_j$. The regularization parameter $\lambda$ controls the prior precision: larger $\lambda$ means a tighter prior, which means more shrinkage toward zero. The ridge solution is exactly the MAP estimate under this Gaussian prior. So every time you tune a ridge penalty, you are implicitly choosing how strongly you believe the coefficients are close to zero.
:::

### When Conjugacy Breaks Down

The four conjugate families in the table above are powerful, but they cover a narrow slice of real problems. Conjugacy breaks down in four common situations:

- The prior and likelihood do not form a conjugate pair (for instance, a Cauchy prior with a Normal likelihood).
- The model involves multiple parameters with complex dependencies (hierarchical models, mixture models).
- The likelihood itself is intractable or defined only through simulation.
- **The model's structure does not match the data's structure.** The Dirichlet-Categorical model for star ratings treats all five levels as unordered categories. This model cannot encode the fact that 5 stars is "better" than 4 stars, which is "better" than 3 stars. An ordinal regression model respects this ordering, but ordinal regression has no conjugate posterior.

In all four cases, no closed-form posterior exists. You need numerical methods to approximate the posterior. The most important class of numerical methods is *Markov chain Monte Carlo* (MCMC), which generates samples from the posterior without ever computing the normalizing constant.

You can now compute posteriors and choose priors for all five headphones quantities. But so far, all the examples have produced clean, closed-form posteriors. What can you *do* with a posterior distribution? The next section answers that question: it shows how posteriors translate into interval estimates, predictions, and decisions.
